fields.label: Order Date
fields.description: The day the shopkeeper placed it, not the day it reached us. A rep syncing at midnight must not have the morning's orders land on tomorrow.

fields.label: Kind
fields.description: What kind of sale this is. Derived, never chosen: the party decides Secondary or Primary, and a primary order dated inside an open season is a Booking of it. Read-only for the same reason the totals are - the server owns it. Deliberately NO default: Frappe backfills every existing row with a Select's default when the column is added, so a default here would have meant the patch that fills this in found nothing empty to fill and silently stamped two primary orders Secondary. It did, once.

fields.label: Season
fields.description: Which season this booking belongs to. Filled by the server from the order date.

fields.label: Rates Locked On
fields.description: When this booking stopped being repriced. A season is booked months before it is delivered, so the price list it was taken from will have moved by then - and a party that booked in November is owed November's price. Set once, at submit, and its presence is what stops a later pricing pass touching the rates.

fields.label: Party Type
fields.description: A shop, or a party we bill ourselves. Exactly one of Outlet and Customer is filled in, and the controller refuses anything else.

fields.label: Customer
fields.description: The party a primary order is for. Blank on a retailer order, where the shop is the party and its distributor is the one billed.

fields.label: Visit
fields.description: The call this order came out of. Left blank on an order taken over the phone, which is why it is not mandatory.

fields.label: Distributor
fields.description: Whose queue this order lands in, and who bills the shop and delivers to it out of their own stock. We never invoice the shop, so the order is terminal in our books and this is where it ends. The limit that matters at the counter is therefore the shop's limit with this distributor - their ledger and not ours, so it can only ever be a soft figure here, one that warns and can route an order for approval while posting nothing. Which limit is actually read, this distributor's or the shop's own account where we are genuinely the seller, is settled in services/credit.py and nowhere else.

fields.label: Status
fields.options:
Draft
Pending Approval
Approved
Sent To Distributor
Accepted
Invoiced
Delivered
Rejected
Cancelled
fields.description: Where the order stands commercially, which docstatus cannot express. An order waiting on a manager and an order already sitting in the distributor's queue are both docstatus 1 and are not remotely the same thing. From Sent To Distributor onward this is the secondary sale running its course at the distributor's end: Invoiced and Delivered are what the distributor reports back to us about a bill they raised on the shop out of their own stock. They are not our accounting, and no state on this list produces a GL Entry.

fields.label: Price List
fields.description: Which list the rates were read from. Stored on the order because the distributor's list can change before the order is delivered, and the rep quoted what he could see.

fields.label: Total Qty
fields.description: Base units across every chargeable line. Server-owned, recomputed on save.

fields.label: Lines
fields.description: Server-owned. Lines-per-call is the number a manager coaches on, so it cannot be a figure the phone supplies.

fields.label: Schemes Applied
fields.description: Written by the server after it re-evaluates the cart. Whatever the phone worked out at the counter is a proposal until this table agrees with it.

fields.label: Gross
fields.description: Server-owned. Every total here is recomputed from the engine on save and overwrites whatever arrived, because the only way to know the phone and the server agree is to work it out again.

fields.label: Discount
fields.description: Server-owned. Scheme discount only - the rep incentive is money for the rep and is kept out of this figure deliberately.

fields.label: Net
fields.description: Server-owned. Gross less discount, floored at zero; an order that computes negative is a scheme misconfiguration, not a refund.

fields.label: Tax
fields.description: Server-owned. An indicative figure so the shopkeeper hears a realistic number at the counter; the Sales Order remains the authority on tax.

fields.label: Grand Total
fields.description: Server-owned. This is the number read back to the shopkeeper, so it is the number that must survive the recomputation unchanged.

fields.label: Rep Incentive
fields.description: Server-owned, and never netted off the bill. Conflating it with discount overstates what the shopkeeper was actually given, which turns into a claim-settlement argument at month end.

fields.label: Phone Said
fields.description: The net the device computed offline, kept exactly as sent. The rep already promised this figure across a counter, so when the server disagrees we need to know which shop heard which number rather than only that something diverged.

fields.label: Engines Agreed
fields.description: Whether the server landed on the same net as the phone. Divergence is not blocked - the order still stands at the server figure - but it is the one signal that says the two engines have drifted apart in the field.

fields.label: Payment Term
fields.options:
Credit
Cash on Delivery
UPI on Delivery
fields.description: How this shop is settling. A shop that has agreed to pay on delivery is not consuming credit, and treating it as though it were blocks orders that were never a risk.

fields.label: Credit Days
fields.description: Defaults from the distributor and can be tightened per order. Never loosened on the device - a longer term than the distributor allows is a decision for a manager, not a phone.

fields.label: Expected Delivery
fields.description: What the rep told the shopkeeper. The distributor delivers on fixed days, so a promise that ignores them is the fastest way to lose a shop's trust.

fields.label: Delivery Instructions
fields.description: Anything the driver needs and the address does not say - shutter closed before noon, deliver to the godown behind, ask for the son.

fields.label: Credit Status
fields.description: Server-owned. A breach is recorded and routed for approval, never refused at the counter: a rep who is blocked in front of a shopkeeper stops booking orders in the app altogether.

fields.label: Limit At Order
fields.description: The limit as it stood when the order was taken. Snapshotted, because a limit raised next week must not retroactively make today's breach disappear.

fields.label: Outstanding At Order
fields.description: What the distributor owed at the moment of capture. Derived later from the ledger it would read differently, and the question being answered is what was true in the market that morning.

fields.label: Needs Approval
fields.description: Set by the server from the approval rules. A device cannot be asked whether it needs permission.

fields.label: Matched Rule
fields.description: Which rule pulled this order in. Without it, an approver sees a queue and no reason for anything being in it.

fields.label: Approval Remarks
fields.description: Why it was let through or turned back. Editable after submit because the decision is routinely made hours after the order synced, with the rep already three shops away.

fields.label: Sent To Distributor On
fields.description: When the order actually reached the distributor's queue, which is not when the shopkeeper placed it. An order taken in a village with no signal is routed hours later on the sync, and the distance between those two timestamps is the only honest measure of how long a shop waits to hear anything back. An approved order still empty here is one nobody has picked up.

fields.label: Distributor Reference
fields.description: The number this order carries in the distributor's own system once they accept it. Filled in by them, never by us. It is what settles a delivery argument, because the shopkeeper and the driver are both holding that number and neither of them has ever seen ours.

fields.label: Confirmed With
fields.description: The name of the person the rep read the order back to. Deliveries get refused by a shop that says nobody ordered this, and a name on the record is what settles it.

fields.label: Sales Order
fields.description: Empty on an order booked at a shop, and that is the ordinary case rather than a gap. A retailer order is a secondary sale: it goes to the distributor, who bills the shop, and the company's own revenue arrives a step later as that distributor's primary order on us - a different document with a different party. This field is filled only where the seller is genuinely us, which means a van sale off the vehicle or an outlet that is billed direct. Raising a Sales Order at booking time would book revenue on a sale the company never made and eat a distributor's credit for stock they never asked for.

fields.label: Client UUID
fields.description: Device-assigned. A replayed push returns this order rather than booking the shop a second one. Not copied on amend, because two documents cannot hold the same identity.

fields.label: App Version
fields.description: Which build proposed the totals. When one version of the phone engine drifts from the server, this is how the affected orders are found rather than guessed at.
